Anatomic Site:Left frontal lobe, (FS)
Clinical Diagnosis/History:
The patient is a 68-year-old man who presented with progressive cognitive decline;
he was given the working diagnosis of
gliomatosis cerebri.  He now undergoes diagnostic biopsy.
Gross Description:
The specimen is received fresh in one part, labeled with the patient's name,
medical record number, and "tumor."  It consists of
three unoriented cores of grayish-white tissue, one measuring 1.0 cm and 0.2
cm in diameter and the others measuring 0.7 cm in
length and 0.2 cm in diameter.  A section is removed from the largest core of
tissue and submitted for cytologic preparation;
the remaining cores are submitted for frozen section diagnosis as FS1, with the
frozen section remnants wrapped in tissue paper and
submitted in cassette B1.  The unfrozen cores of tissue are wrapped in tissue
paper and submitted in cassette B2.
Diagnosis Comments:
Both sections B1 and B2 show a diffusely infiltrating population of relatively
uniform oligodendrocytes involving white matter
consistent with frontal lobe, with neoplastic satellitosis and infiltration along
vessels (best demonstrated on Slide B2).  No
mitoses are identified, and significant nuclear pleomorphism is not present.
Foci of microvascular proliferation and necrosis
are absent.  Immunohistochemical stains are performed and examined at Stanford
Medical Center to establish the diagnosis on Slide B2, including
GFAP, CD45, and Ki-67.  These show only a rare benign GFAP positive
astrocyte, and only a few CD45 positive lymphocytes.  A Ki-67
labeling index will be performed and reported in an addendum.

Interoperative Diagnosis:
FS1  (B) Brain, left frontal lobe, core biopsy:  Cytologic preparation
favors a diagnosis of infiltrating oligodendroglioma, grade
II; single core frozen shows oligodendrogliosis.  Tissue section and cytologic
preparation.  (Dr. Susan Clark, 30214.)
Final Diagnosis:
Left frontal lobe, stereotactic biopsy:  Oligodendroglioma, WHO grade II.

COMMENT:
Histological examination of the left frontal lobe reveals diffuse infiltration by atypical glial cells with an astrocytic phenotype. The infiltrative pattern is consistent with gliomatosis cerebri, WHO Grade II. Immunohistochemistry shows positive staining for GFAP and negative for IDH1 R132H. The Ki-67 proliferation index is low, approximately 3%. No necrosis or microvascular proliferation is observed. The molecular profile suggests a low-grade glioma without IDH mutation.
The right temporal and parietal lobes show similar histological features, confirming the diagnosis of gliomatosis cerebri. The cerebellum biopsy shows no evidence of tumor involvement.
The diagnosis of gliomatosis cerebri is based on the extensive involvement of multiple lobes with glial tumor cells. The tumor is not amenable to surgical resection, and management will focus on adjunctive therapies.
